> 損。有孚，元吉，無咎，可貞，利有攸往。曷之用？二簋可用享。

Hexagram 41 is about taking something away, and it hands out four favourable judgements before it says what it is.

## 損 is a hand

說文: 損，減也。從手，員聲.

Built on 手 — a hand, taking something off.

And the previous hexagram, 解, is built on 刀 — a knife, opening something.

Two adjacent hexagrams, two adjacent characters, two actions: cut open, and take away. The 易 placed them next to each other, and both are verbs of ending something.

## Four good verdicts on a subtraction

有孚，元吉，無咎，可貞，利有攸往.

Four favourable judgements in a row, which is very rare. And the thing they describe is a removal.

So the 易's position here is as counterintuitive as it is stated plainly: subtraction can be very good.

## 曷之用？二簋可用享

Asked and answered in the same judgement — one of the few places the book asks itself a question.

曷: what. 之: this way of 損. 用: to apply.

How is this 損 to be used?

二簋: two simple baskets of offering. 享: to present.

Two baskets are enough to present.

Which sets the standard the whole chapter works at: what makes an offering acceptable is not its quantity, and the reduction of quantity does not make it worse.

## 三人行 / 一人行

六三 三人行，則損一人；一人行，則得其友.

Three walking together will lose one; one walking alone will find a friend.

Which reads as an arithmetic that doesn't add: going alone is how a companion is obtained, and going in a group is how one is lost.

And it is the hexagram's most exact statement of what subtraction does — the third person is not an accident or a casualty. Removing one from three is what makes two able to be one pair.

## 惩忿窒欲

The 象: 君子以懲忿窒欲.

懲 is to check, to restrain. 窒 is to stop up, to block.

Two characters, two directions: 忿 is anger, which rushes outward; 欲 is desire, which draws inward. One plugs the exit, one plugs the intake.

Which is the practical form of 損, and it says what kind of thing is being removed: not possessions. The two things that will not stay in their places.

## 已事遄往

初九 已事遄往，無咎，酌損之.

遄: swift. When the matter is done, go swiftly.

And 酌損之: measure the reduction.

So the first line already supplies the discipline the whole chapter needs: subtract quickly when the moment arrives, and subtract by measure when you do.

## 損其疾

六四: reduce one's illness.

疾 here is not the body's but the character's — a habit, a fault, an error of one's own.

And 使遄有喜: let it be quick, and there is good.

Which is the same word as the first line's 遄: swiftness is the hexagram's repeated requirement, once for departure, once for cure.

## Ten pairs of shells

六五 或益之，十朋之龜，弗克違，元吉.

朋: two strings of shells (or five, depending on the account). 十朋之龜: an oracle turtle of great value.

A thing so evidently right that even the turtle cannot contradict it.

## The test

Take something you are considering giving up — a commitment, a possession, a way of being needed. Ask the question the judgement asks: what is this 損 for? The chapter's answer is not "less is better." It is: two baskets are enough, and the reduction has a measure.
